analysis.one_liner: Requires nearly all employers to provide paid vacation leave, earned one hour for every 25 worked, up to 80 hours a year.
analysis.headline: The bill, which would give workers up to 80 hours of paid leave a year, was referred to five House committees and has had no further action.
analysis.plain_summary: The Protected Time Off Act would require nearly every employer in the country, including governments, to give workers paid vacation: one hour earned for every 25 hours worked, up to 80 hours (two weeks) per year. Workers could use the leave for any reason, could not be forced to explain why or find their own replacement, could carry over up to 40 hours, and would be paid out for unused leave when they leave a job. Employers could still deny a specific requested date for a real business reason, as long as they offer an alternative time within 30 days. Workers could sue to enforce the law, with attorney's fees and extra damages, and the Labor Department could investigate and take employers to court.
analysis.who_benefits: Working people, especially the roughly one in four private-sector workers who get no paid vacation and the low-wage, part-time, and service workers least likely to have it. Tipped workers are guaranteed paid leave at least at the applicable minimum wage, and workers at every employer size (even one employee) are covered. Employers who already offer generous leave also gain a level playing field, because competitors can no longer skip the benefit to cut costs.

how_it_helps.text: Employers must provide at least 1 hour of paid annual leave for every 25 hours worked, up to 80 hours in a 12-month period, and employees begin earning it on their first day.

Leave can be used for any reason, workers cannot be forced to explain why they need it or to find their own replacement, and employers cannot count leave use against a no-fault attendance policy or use it in hiring, promotion, or discipline.
If a worker leaves a job with unused leave, the employer must pay it out; workers also carry over up to 40 unused hours to the next year.
The bill is enforceable: workers can sue for lost wages plus liquidated damages and attorney's fees, and the Labor Department can investigate, subpoena records, and sue violators.

analysis.who_pays: Employers, who must pay wages for leave time, pay out unused leave at separation, track accruals, and post notices. Small businesses face the same requirements as large ones, though they may already offer some leave. Costs may be passed to consumers through prices.

drawbacks.text: The mandate is capped at 80 hours (two weeks) of paid leave per year and allows carryover of only 40 hours, so it sets a floor rather than the more generous minimums some European countries or some state and local laws already provide.

Employers can deny a requested leave date for a 'bona fide business reason' as long as they offer an alternative date within 30 days, which gives businesses real scheduling control; workers on fixed schedules or with rigid child-care arrangements may find the alternative times unusable.

Employers bear the direct cost of paying wages for leave not worked plus new notice, posting, and accrual-tracking systems, and small businesses in particular will face compliance costs; some of that cost will be passed to consumers or absorbed in slower hiring.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit to workers is large and concrete: a guaranteed, enforceable federal vacation entitlement where none exists today, with real teeth (private lawsuits, liquidated damages, attorney's fees). The main cost falls on employers as paid time and compliance paperwork, and it will be passed partly into prices and partly absorbed in reduced hiring flexibility. The scheduling-flexibility provisions are drafted to let businesses manage coverage, which blunts the objection that firms cannot operate, but small firms employing even one person are covered and will feel the compliance burden most.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to five different House committees when introduced, and none of them has taken it up, so it sits with no scheduled hearing, markup, or vote.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on July 25, 2025, and referred to five House committees: Education and Workforce, House Administration, Oversight and Government Reform, Judiciary, and Transportation and Infrastructure.
As of the end of the provided record, no committee has held a markup, reported the bill, or scheduled it for a floor vote; the only actions in the history are introduction and referral.
The bill has 86 cosponsors, all of them Democrats.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, employers who do not provide paid vacation are better off, because no mandate has moved toward becoming law. Workers without paid leave have gained nothing yet, though the bill remains technically alive.

for.name: 86 Democratic cosponsors
for.role: House cosponsors including Reps. Adams, Casar, Jayapal, Khanna, and McGovern
for.what_they_did: Signed on as cosponsors; all 86 are Democrats.

sides.party_line_note: All 86 cosponsors are Democrats and no Republicans have signed on, so support for the bill so far splits entirely along party lines.

industries.industry: Employers without paid vacation (retail, food service, hospitality, small businesses)
industries.note: Employers that currently offer no paid vacation must pay wages for up to 80 hours a year of leave and add tracking and notice systems. These are the industries with the most hourly, low-wage workers, so the mandate is felt most sharply there.

State government employers are covered, and the bill seeks to waive sovereign immunity for state employees' suits, which states typically contest in court. Public agencies already often provide leave, so the practical cost may be modest.

industries.industry: Businesses that already offer generous paid leave
industries.note: Firms with richer leave policies gain a level playing field: the bill sets a floor that prevents rivals from undercutting them by denying workers any paid time off. Existing state laws with greater rights are preserved.

analysis.trajectory: Bills referred to five committees rarely reach the floor, and this one has no Republican cosponsors in a Republican-controlled House, so the most likely path is that it stays in committee and expires at the end of the 119th Congress without a vote, as most mandatory paid-leave bills have. Its cosponsor count gives it visibility but no vehicle for floor action.
